docs.title: FitForge
docs.text:
AI-Based Student Sports Talent & Fitness Guidance Portal

From raw fitness data to coach-approved sports guidance.

Team: Kiratpreet Kaur (1024030402) · Prisha Goyal (1024030404) — Batch 3C31

docs.title: What is FitForge?
docs.text:
Schools run fitness tests regularly, but the results usually end up in a notebook or a spreadsheet and go nowhere. FitForge takes a student's general fitness assessment and turns it into two things a school can actually use:

  1. An explainable, leakage-checked fitness-level prediction.
  2. Sport-suitability guidance — 2–3 recommended sports with a plain-language reason.

Every prediction is held back from students and parents until a coach explicitly approves or overrides it — the model assists, it never decides.

docs.title: Core design principle: Two-Tier data strategy
docs.text:
• Tier 1 — General Athleticism (current scope): a single universal fitness battery for every student, used to recommend suitable sports.
  • Tier 2 — Sport-Specific KPIs (future scope): a small, per-sport indicator set for students funnelled into a specific sport squad, added incrementally once Tier 1 is stable.

This split exists specifically to avoid a system that is too complex for a coach to actually use — see Scope for the full reasoning.

docs.title: Layered Architecture
docs.text: Layer Responsibility Frontend React/Next.js — separate views for Student, Coach, Admin, Parent Backend API Node.js/Express — auth, validation, orchestration ML Service Python, Pandas, scikit-learn — model training/inference Database PostgreSQL (relational — see Database Design) Reporting Chart.js/Recharts for visualizations; PDF export Authentication JWT / role-based access

docs.title: Data Flow (High Level)
docs.text:
Coach enters assessment (Frontend)
        |
   Backend API validates + stores in Assessments table
        |
   ML Service reads Assessment record
        |
   ML Service returns prediction (fitness_level, sport, focus, reason)
        |
   Backend API writes prediction into Recommendations table (coach_approved = false)
        |
   Coach reviews on Coach Dashboard -> approves or overrides
        |
   Student/Parent view unlocks once coach_approved = true

docs.title: The Model ↔ Database Contract
docs.text:
This is the single most important agreement between the two halves of the team (ML owner and Database owner). If both sides build to this exact contract, the two parts can be developed independently and plugged together at the end without rework.

Input to the model (read from the Assessments table): 

age_group, height_cm, weight_kg, bmi, sprint_time_sec, shuttle_run_sec,
pushups_count, situps_count, plank_time_sec, broad_jump_cm,
flexibility_score, attendance_rate, coach_rating

Output from the model (written into the Recommendations table): 

predicted_fitness_level, recommended_sport, improvement_focus, model_confidence

docs.title: Why PostgreSQL (Relational, Not NoSQL)
docs.text: The data is inherently relational: one student has many assessments, one assessment has one (or a small versioned set of) recommendations, and coaches/admins need role-based joins across these. A relational schema makes progress-tracking queries ("show this student's history," "show all Low Performers needing follow-up") straightforward with standard SQL, rather than needing manual document restructuring in a NoSQL store.

docs.title: Security & Access Control Notes
docs.text:
• All roles (Student, Coach, Admin, Parent) authenticate via JWT.
  • Students have read-only access to their own records only.
  • Coaches have read/write access to their assigned students' assessments and recommendation approvals.
  • No recommendation is exposed outside the Coach role until coach_approved = true (enforced at the API layer, not just the UI, to prevent bypass).

docs.title: Current Implementation Status
docs.text: The frontend, ML service, and coach-approval workflow are implemented and working end-to-end. Assessments are currently persisted in a flat, interim structure rather than the full relational schema above — migrating to PostgreSQL is the next planned increment (see Scope).

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Database Design
docs.text: Owner: Prisha Goyal

docs.title: Why This Structure
docs.text: Each student is assessed multiple times (every 4–8 weeks). So the database cannot store "one row per student" — it must store one row per assessment, linked back to the student. This is what enables progress charts and improvement percentages later.

docs.title: Students
docs.text:
One row per student. Static/rarely-changing info only.

Column Type Notes student_id INT/UUID, PK anonymous_code VARCHAR Used instead of real name for privacy (e.g. "STU-0001") age_group VARCHAR e.g. "9th", "10th" gender VARCHAR Optional sport_interest VARCHAR Student's stated preference medical_clearance_status VARCHAR e.g. "Cleared", "Restricted" — not a full medical record created_at TIMESTAMP

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
One row per fitness-test event — the core table.

Column Type Notes assessment_id INT/UUID, PK student_id FK -> Students assessment_date DATE height_cm, weight_kg, bmi FLOAT BMI can be calculated sprint_time_sec, shuttle_run_sec FLOAT pushups_count, situps_count INT plank_time_sec, broad_jump_cm FLOAT flexibility_score FLOAT attendance_rate FLOAT % attendance leading up to this assessment coach_rating INT 1–10 subjective rating created_by_coach_id FK -> Coaches

docs.title: Coaches
docs.text: Column Type coach_id INT/UUID, PK name VARCHAR assigned_sports VARCHAR

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
One row per ML prediction — where the model's output is stored.

Column Type Notes recommendation_id INT/UUID, PK assessment_id FK -> Assessments predicted_fitness_level VARCHAR Beginner / Developing / Good / Excellent recommended_sport VARCHAR improvement_focus VARCHAR model_confidence FLOAT Optional coach_approved BOOLEAN Mandatory gate before student/parent visibility coach_override_value VARCHAR If coach manually changes the recommendation created_at TIMESTAMP

docs.title: Admins (optional, for early RBAC)
docs.text: Column Type admin_id INT/UUID, PK name VARCHAR role VARCHAR — "admin" / "coach" / "student" / "parent"

docs.title: Relationships (ER Diagram — Text Form)
docs.text:
Students (1) ----< (many) Assessments
Coaches  (1) ----< (many) Assessments        [via created_by_coach_id]
Assessments (1) ---< (many) Recommendations  [usually 1, but allow many for versioning]

docs.title: SQL (PostgreSQL, ready to run)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE Coaches (
    coach_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    assigned_sports VARCHAR(200)
);

CREATE TABLE Students (
    student_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    anonymous_code VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    age_group VARCHAR(10),
    gender VARCHAR(20),
    sport_interest VARCHAR(50),
    medical_clearance_status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Cleared',
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE Assessments (
    assessment_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    student_id INT REFERENCES Students(student_id),
    assessment_date DATE NOT NULL,
    height_cm FLOAT,
    weight_kg FLOAT,
    bmi FLOAT,
    sprint_time_sec FLOAT,
    shuttle_run_sec FLOAT,
    pushups_count INT,
    situps_count INT,
    plank_time_sec FLOAT,
    broad_jump_cm FLOAT,
    flexibility_score FLOAT,
    attendance_rate FLOAT,
    coach_rating INT CHECK (coach_rating BETWEEN 1 AND 10),
    created_by_coach_id INT REFERENCES Coaches(coach_id)
);

CREATE TABLE Recommendations (
    recommendation_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    assessment_id INT REFERENCES Assessments(assessment_id),
    predicted_fitness_level VARCHAR(20),
    recommended_sport VARCHAR(50),
    improvement_focus VARCHAR(50),
    model_confidence FLOAT,
    coach_approved BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    coach_override_value VARCHAR(50),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE Admins (
    admin_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    role VARCHAR(20) CHECK (role IN ('admin','coach','student','parent'))
);

docs.title: Database Owner's Task List
docs.text:
1. Set up PostgreSQL and run the SQL above.
  2. Build a small API layer (Node.js/Express or Python/FastAPI) with: - add_student() - add_assessment(student_id, ...) - get_assessment_history(student_id) — for progress charts - save_recommendation(assessment_id, prediction_data) — the ML model calls this - approve_recommendation(recommendation_id, coach_id)
  3. Seed the database with ~50–100 synthetic students, each with 2–3 assessments, for realistic testing.
  4. Sync the exact input/output column format with the ML owner (see System Architecture).
  5. Document the final ER diagram and schema for the report (satisfies "Data Modeling through E-R Diagram" in the syllabus).

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text: Assessments are currently persisted in a flat, interim structure rather than this full relational schema. Migrating to the schema above is the next planned increment — see Scope.

docs.title: Sprint Plan (Agile/Scrum)
docs.text:
• Sprint 1: Requirements, personas, schema design, use cases.
  • Sprint 2: Authentication, role-based access, database setup (all 5 tables).
  • Sprint 3: Fitness Assessment module (entry, validation, BMI/improvement calculation).
  • Sprint 4: ML baseline model (Decision Tree/Random Forest), trained and evaluated on chosen dataset.
  • Sprint 5: Coach Dashboard — review, approve, override recommendations.
  • Sprint 6: Performance & Progress Reports (charts, PDF export).
  • Sprint 7: Admin Dashboard and school-wide analytics.
  • Sprint 8: Integration, usability testing, final demonstration.

Backlog is built directly from the Must/Should/Could priority tags in Requirements.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Unit testing: BMI/improvement calculations, validation rules, RBAC checks.
  • Model evaluation: accuracy, precision/recall per class, confusion matrix; explicit check for data leakage and class imbalance before reporting results (see ML Model Plan for why this matters).
  • Integration testing: assessment entry -> model prediction -> coach approval -> student/parent visibility flow.
  • Usability testing: whether coaches and parents can interpret reports and recommendations without guidance.
  • Security testing: role-based access boundaries (e.g., a student cannot access another student's data).

docs.title: ML Model Plan
docs.text: Owner: Kiratpreet Kaur

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Start with simple, explainable models — chosen specifically so results can be defended in a project viva:

Model Purpose Decision Tree Easy to explain and visualize; primary baseline Random Forest Higher accuracy, feature importance ranking KNN Recommends sports by comparing similar fitness profiles

docs.title: Input Features
docs.text: age_group, height, weight, BMI, sprint_time, shuttle_run, pushups, situps, plank_time, broad_jump, flexibility, attendance, sport_interest, coach_rating

docs.title: Output Labels
docs.text: fitness_level (Beginner / Developing / Good / Excellent), recommended_sport, improvement_focus

docs.title: Model Flow
docs.text:
Fitness-test data + preference + coach assessment
                    |
              Data cleaning
                    |
       ML model prediction/recommendation
                    |
 Coach reviews/approves recommendation
                    |
Training plan and periodic reassessment
                    |
        Progress report and new data

Governing rule: the model is a coach-support tool. No prediction reaches a student or parent without coach approval or override.

docs.title: Real Findings From Baseline Testing
docs.text: An actual baseline test was run on a public student PE dataset (500 rows, Kaggle). Three concrete lessons came out of it and now shape the model design:

docs.title: 1. Data leakage inflates accuracy artificially
docs.text:
An initial run included a column called Overall_PE_Performance_Score as an input feature. Result: 98% accuracy — suspiciously high. Feature importance analysis showed the model relying almost entirely on that one derived column (and Attendance_Rate), while genuine fitness scores (Strength, Endurance, Flexibility, Speed) had zero importance. This happened because the "overall score" column was itself derived from the same data used to create the target label.

Lesson applied: never include a summary/derived score as a model input. Only raw, independently-collected test values feed the model.

docs.title: 2. Phase 3 retraining uses a reproducible, leakage-controlled evaluation
docs.text:
The Phase 3 training script uses the original 500 labelled rows only, drops the identifier and label-derived fields (ID, Performance, Overall_PE_Performance_Score, Improvement_Rate, and Final_Grade), and creates one fixed 80/20 stratified split (random_state=42). Numeric columns are median-imputed and scaled; categorical columns are most-frequent-imputed and one-hot encoded inside each pipeline.

Logistic Regression, a shallow Decision Tree, and Random Forest were evaluated both before and after sigmoid probability calibration. The calibrated Decision Tree was selected by macro-F1, rather than overall accuracy, because accuracy disguises minority-class failure:

Metric on the untouched 100-row holdout Selected calibrated Decision Tree Accuracy 84.0% Balanced accuracy 57.1% Macro-F1 0.565 Expected calibration error 0.074

The repeatable script, JSON evaluation report, and confusion matrix live in code/ml/src/train_fitness_model.py and code/ml/reports/.

docs.title: 3. Attendance and motivation emerged as the strongest genuine predictors
docs.text:
Class-wise average attendance showed a clean, monotonic pattern:

Performance Class Avg. Attendance High Performer 94.2% Average Performer 89.8% Low Performer 84.7%

This was stronger and cleaner than any raw physical-fitness score at separating the classes — a legitimate, report-ready insight: "Attendance and engagement emerged as strong predictors of PE performance — even more than raw physical fitness scores — suggesting consistency matters as much as raw ability."

docs.title: 4. Class imbalance is a known, unresolved limitation
docs.text:
The High Performer category has only 12 out of 500 records (2.4%), which produces only two High Performer cases in the fixed holdout set. The selected model has 0% recall for that class on this test. That means 84% accuracy must not be described as talent-identification accuracy. The application returns calibrated probabilities and marks each prediction for coach review, but it must not claim that it can reliably identify high-potential athletes yet.

Recommended handling for the report: document this honestly as a known limitation, and consider one of:

  • Collapsing to two categories ("Needs Improvement" vs. "Meeting/ Exceeding Expectations") to avoid an unreliable third class.
  • Collecting more independently assessed High Performer records before enabling athlete-selection decisions.

docs.title: What This Means Going Forward
docs.text:
• Whichever final dataset is used, repeat this same leakage check before trusting any accuracy number.
  • Report both the "before" and "after" leakage-correction numbers where space allows — it demonstrates methodological rigor to an examiner.
  • Treat the model as a decision-support signal, not a verdict — this is already baked into the requirement that coaches must approve/override every output (see Requirements, FR-05/FR-06).

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text: Sport-suitability recommendation logic is specified but not yet implemented — the current system predicts a fitness category only. This is the next planned increment (see Scope).

docs.title: What FitForge Is
docs.text:
A web-based decision-support platform that digitizes school fitness assessments, tracks student athletic performance over time, and uses an explainable ML model to recommend suitable sports and training focus areas — with mandatory coach review before any recommendation reaches a student or parent.

One-line positioning: "FitForge takes raw, unorganized fitness data and forges it into clear, coach-approved sports guidance."

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Schools conduct sports activities, but student fitness and performance data is rarely recorded systematically or analyzed over time. As a result:

  • Students with real sports potential can go unnoticed.
  • Interested students don't receive personalized, data-backed guidance on which sport suits them or what to improve.
  • Progress isn't tracked consistently, so improvement (or decline) goes unmeasured.
  • Coaches lack a structured way to compare students across age groups, fitness levels, or improvement needs.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Digitize fitness-test and sports-performance records per student.
  • Track individual improvement over successive assessments (every 4–8 weeks).
  • Predict a fitness category using an explainable ML model.
  • Recommend a suitable sport and improvement focus, always with a stated reason.
  • Require coach review/approval before any recommendation is acted on.
  • Generate clear, exportable reports for students, parents, coaches, and admins.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• FitForge does not determine a student's future or talent on its own — the model is coach-support only.
  • FitForge does not replace certified PE curriculum, professional talent scouting, or medical evaluation.
  • FitForge does not collect or process real medical records — only a simple clearance/restriction status.
  • FitForge does not claim scientific certainty in its recommendations; outputs are guidance, not verdicts.

docs.title: Who Uses It
docs.text: Persona Role Access Student Views own fitness report, recommended sport, training plan, progress Read-only, own data Coach/PE Teacher Enters assessments, evaluates skills, reviews/approves or overrides AI recommendations Read/write, assigned students School Admin Manages students, coaches, sports catalog, and system-wide reports Full access, admin scope Parent Optionally views their child's progress and recommendations Read-only, own child's data

docs.title: Why This Is a Strong Software Engineering Project
docs.text: It combines full-stack development, relational database design, applied machine learning, role-based security, data visualization, and reporting — all wrapped around a real, socially useful problem. It also forces genuine engineering discipline: coach-approval gating, explainability requirements, and honest handling of dataset limitations (see ML Model Plan) rather than presenting AI as an infallible black box.

docs.title: Key Modules
docs.text:
1. Authentication & Roles — Role-based login for Student, Coach, Admin, Parent. Students cannot edit their own official assessment data.
  2. Fitness Assessment — Coach enters raw test scores; system validates, stores history, auto-calculates BMI and improvement %.
  3. ML Recommendation System — Predicts fitness category, recommends a sport and improvement focus, always with a stated reason.
  4. Personalized Guidance — Weekly training plan, numeric goals, attendance tracker, scheduled reassessment.
  5. Performance & Progress Reports — Charts, comparison against own history, downloadable PDF, coach remarks.
  6. Coach Dashboard — Filter/view assigned students, review/override AI recommendations.
  7. Admin Dashboard — School-wide distribution analytics, follow-up tracking.

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text: ID Priority Requirement FR-01 Must The system shall allow a coach to record a fitness assessment for a student, including all core test scores. FR-02 Must The system shall auto-calculate BMI and improvement percentage from the prior assessment. FR-03 Must The system shall predict a fitness level and recommended sport using the trained ML model. FR-04 Must Every prediction shall include a plain-language reason for the recommendation. FR-05 Must No prediction shall be visible to a student or parent until a coach approves or overrides it. FR-06 Must The system shall allow a coach to override any AI-generated recommendation. FR-07 Must The system shall support Student, Coach, Admin, and Parent roles with distinct access permissions. FR-08 Must Students shall not be able to edit their own official assessment data. FR-09 Should The system shall generate a downloadable PDF progress report per student. FR-10 Should The system shall display comparison charts (speed, stamina, strength, flexibility, attendance) against the student's own prior results. FR-11 Should The coach dashboard shall support filtering students by sport, age group, fitness level, or improvement need. FR-12 Should The admin dashboard shall show school-wide distribution analytics (fitness level, sport interest, follow-up needs). FR-13 Could The system shall recommend exercise videos/articles relevant to a student's improvement focus. FR-14 Could Parents shall be able to view a read-only summary of their child's progress.

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text: Category Requirement Privacy Use anonymized/synthetic data for development; store only clearance status, not full medical records; minimum data collection principle. Security Role-based access control; authenticated sessions; students restricted from editing official records. Explainability Every ML output must show the reasoning/features behind the recommendation, not a bare label. Fairness/Reliability The model shall not be presented as determining a student's talent or future; coach approval is mandatory before any output is acted upon. Usability Dashboards and reports must be understandable by coaches and parents without technical background. Performance Assessment entry and prediction retrieval should complete within a few seconds for a responsive coach workflow. Data Integrity Assessment history must be immutable once approved (append new assessments rather than overwrite past ones), to preserve accurate progress tracking.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• A coach can enter a full assessment and see BMI and improvement % auto-calculated.
  • A test assessment produces a fitness-level prediction, a recommended sport, and a stated reason.
  • A prediction is not visible to the student/parent view until a coach has approved or overridden it.
  • A student can view their own progress chart showing at least two assessments over time.
  • Role-based access prevents a student from editing their own assessment record.
  • An admin can view school-wide distribution by fitness level.

docs.title: Requirements Traceability
docs.text: Requirement Module Acceptance Evidence FR-01, FR-02 Fitness Assessment Assessment saved with auto-calculated BMI/improvement % FR-03, FR-04 ML Recommendation System Prediction includes level, sport, and stated reason FR-05, FR-06 Coach Dashboard Recommendation hidden from student view until approved/overridden FR-07, FR-08 Authentication & Roles Role-restricted access verified per user type FR-09, FR-10 Performance & Progress Reports PDF export and comparison chart render correctly FR-11 Coach Dashboard Filter by sport/age/fitness level returns correct subset FR-12 Admin Dashboard Distribution analytics match underlying data

docs.title: Explicitly Out of Scope
docs.text:
• Real medical diagnosis or detailed medical record storage.
  • Fully automated decisions that bypass coach review.
  • Professional talent-scouting guarantees or claims of predicting future athletic success.
  • Live web-scraped exercise content (use a curated local catalogue instead).
  • Collection of real students' personally identifying information (names, Aadhaar, phone numbers) for ML training.
  • Integration with official Khelo India private student records.

docs.title: Not Yet Delivered, and Why
docs.text:
Reported plainly rather than implied as complete:

  • Sport-suitability recommendation logic (mapping a fitness profile to specific suggested sports) is specified but not yet implemented; the current system predicts a fitness category only.
  • Relational database migration: assessments are currently persisted in a flat structure rather than the normalised PostgreSQL schema described in Database Design; this is the next planned increment.

docs.title: Future Scope
docs.text:
• Tier 2 rollout: sport-specific KPI tracking for squad-selected students, added one sport at a time, each with its own 5–7 KPIs and a progression/forecasting model.
  • Expand from a synthetic/public dataset to real, consented school data for validation.
  • Address class-imbalance properly (oversampling, or collapsing fitness- level categories) once more data is available.
  • Multi-school deployment with school-level comparative analytics.
  • Mobile app version for coaches to enter assessments pitch-side.
  • Injury-risk flagging based on load/attendance patterns (with clear non-medical disclaimers).

docs.title: Assumptions & Constraints
docs.text:
• Student prototype only; not a production deployment.
  • Dataset used for training is a public/synthetic dataset with known, documented limitations (leakage risk, class imbalance — see ML Model Plan).
  • Two-person team: ML model and database development proceed in parallel against a fixed interface contract (System Architecture).
  • Real-world use would require school administrative approval, parental consent processes, and data-protection review beyond course scope.
